claim: Wnt plays important role during development and in various diseases.
source: Wnt plays important role during development and in various diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Wnts are lipidated and highly hydrophobic.
source: Because Wnts are lipidated and highly hydrophobic, they can only be purified in the presence of detergents, limiting their use in various in vitro and in vivo assays.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Wnt protein properties.

claim: Wnts can only be purified in the presence of detergents.
source: Because Wnts are lipidated and highly hydrophobic, they can only be purified in the presence of detergents, limiting their use in various in vitro and in vivo assays.
evidence: This statement reflects the conventional understanding prior to the current study's findings.

claim: Wnt3a co-purified with a glycoprotein afamin derived from bovine serum.
source: We purified N-terminally tagged recombinant Wnt3a secreted from cells and accidentally discovered that Wnt3a co-purified with a glycoprotein afamin derived from the bovine serum included in the media.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Wnt3a forms a 1:1 complex with afamin.
source: Wnt3a forms a 1:1 complex with afamin, which remains soluble in aqueous buffer after isolation, and can induce signaling in various cellular systems including the intestical stem cell growth assay.
evidence: This is supported by SEC data in Figure 4 showing stoichiometric complex formation.

claim: The Wnt3a-afamin complex remains soluble in aqueous buffer after isolation.
source: Wnt3a forms a 1:1 complex with afamin, which remains soluble in aqueous buffer after isolation, and can induce signaling in various cellular systems including the intestical stem cell growth assay.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SEC experiments in detergent-free buffer shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Wnt3a-afamin complex can induce signaling in various cellular systems including the intestinal stem cell growth assay.
source: Wnt3a forms a 1:1 complex with afamin, which remains soluble in aqueous buffer after isolation, and can induce signaling in various cellular systems including the intestical stem cell growth assay.
evidence: This is supported by the TCF reporter assay data in Figure 5A and organoid culture data in Figure 5B.

claim: Biologically active afamin-Wnt complex can be easily obtained in large quantity by co-expressing with afamin.
source: By co-expressing with afamin, biologically active afamin-Wnt complex can be easily obtained in large quantity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the large-scale production experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Afamin can solubilize Wnt5a, Wnt3, and many more Wnt subtypes.
source: As afamin can also solubilize Wnt5a, Wnt3, and many more Wnt subtypes, afamin complexation will open a way to put various Wnt ligands and their signaling mechanisms under a thorough biochemical scrutiny that had been difficult for years.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6 and 7 showing multiple Wnt proteins can be solubilized by afamin.

claim: At least 19 Wnt proteins are present in mammals.
source: At least 19 Wnt proteins are present in mammals, each serving different but potentially overlapping functions (Holstein, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Holstein, 2012.

claim: All mammalian Wnts are predicted to be covalently lipidated at a conserved Ser residue.
source: All mammalian Wnts are predicted to be covalently lipidated at a conserved Ser residue (Takada et al., 2006; Willert et al., 2003), a modification essential to their biological activity because of its contribution to the interaction with Frizzled receptors (Janda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takada et al., 2006 and Willert et al., 2003.

claim: Lipidation is essential to Wnt biological activity because of its contribution to the interaction with Frizzled receptors.
source: All mammalian Wnts are predicted to be covalently lipidated at a conserved Ser residue (Takada et al., 2006; Willert et al., 2003), a modification essential to their biological activity because of its contribution to the interaction with Frizzled receptors (Janda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Janda et al., 2012.

claim: Purified Wnt proteins tend to lose their biological activity, probably due to aggregation even in the presence of detergents.
source: Due to the strong hydrophobic property granted by the lipid moiety, however, purified Wnt proteins tend to lose their biological activity, probably due to the aggregation even in the presence of detergents (Dhamdhere et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dhamdhere et al., 2014.

claim: Wnt secretion from cultured cells requires the presence of bovine serum in the media.
source: Curiously, it has been known that Wnt secretion from cultured cells require the presence of bovine serum in the media (Willert, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Willert, 2008.

claim: The serum component(s) that support Wnt secretion has not been identified prior to this study.
source: The serum component(s) that support Wnt secretion has not been identified, and it is generally assumed that serum lipids render the hydrophobic Wnt proteins soluble.
evidence: This statement describes the state of knowledge before the current study.

claim: CHAPS-solubilized Wnt quickly loses its biological activity upon incubation at 37°C, unless it is reconstituted into lipid vesicle.
source: Moreover, CHAPS-solubilized Wnt quickly loses its biological activity upon incubation at 37°C, unless it is reconstituted into lipid vesicle (Dhamdhere et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dhamdhere et al., 2014.

claim: Afamin is responsible for the aqueous partitioning of Wnt proteins rather than lipid molecules.
source: In the present report, we identified the serum component responsible for the aqueous partitioning of Wnt proteins as a serum glycoprotein afamin rather than lipid molecules.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Afamin-Wnt complex is decomposed upon the addition of 1% CHAPS.
source: Afamin and Wnt apparently makes 1:1 complex in the culture media, which is highly soluble in detergent-free buffers upon isolation but is decomposed upon the addition of 1% CHAPS.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SEC experiments in Figure 4 comparing +/- CHAPS conditions.

claim: Afamin-Wnt complex is biologically active.
source: Afamin-Wnt complex is biologically active, indicating that afamin can deliver Wnt ligands to its receptors on cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by the reporter assay data in Figure 5A and organoid culture data in Figure 5B.

claim: Afamin can deliver Wnt ligands to its receptors on cell surface.
source: Afamin-Wnt complex is biologically active, indicating that afamin can deliver Wnt ligands to its receptors on cell surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the biological activity of the complex in cell-based assays.

claim: Large quantity of biologically active Wnt3a, Wnt5a, and Wnt3 proteins can be prepared using afamin as a carrier.
source: By using afamin as a carrier, we succeeded in preparing large quantity of biologically active Wnt3a, Wnt5a, and Wnt3 proteins with no other components, which can be stored at 4°C.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the large-scale purification data in Figure 8.

claim: Afamin-Wnt complexes can be stored at 4°C.
source: By using afamin as a carrier, we succeeded in preparing large quantity of biologically active Wnt3a, Wnt5a, and Wnt3 proteins with no other components, which can be stored at 4°C.
evidence: This is supported by the stability data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: N-terminal addition of the 21-residue 'TARGET(Tg)' tag is compatible with Wnt3a expression and secretion.
source: We first systematically explored the tagging condition for the expression and secretion of mouse Wnt3a in HEK cells, and found that N-terminal addition of the 21-residue 'TARGET(Tg)' tag developed in our lab (Tabata et al., 2010) (see schematics in Supplementary file 1) was compatible.
evidence: This is supported by the Western blot and reporter assay data in Figure 1.

claim: Conditioned medium from HEK cells stably expressing Tg-Wnt3a contained Wnt3a antigen at a level comparable to that from L-3a cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, conditioned medium (CM) from HEK cells stably expressing Tg-Wnt3a contained Wnt3a antigen at a level comparable to that from L-3a cells.
evidence: This is directly shown in the Western blot data in Figure 1A.

claim: Both CM from L-3a and Tg-Wnt3a/HEK cells possessed similar activity in the Wnt reporter assay.
source: The Wnt reporter assay revealed that both CM possessed similar activity (Figure 1B), indicating that the N-terminal tagging did not impair the biological activity of Wnt3a that had been successfully secreted into the media.
evidence: This is shown in the reporter assay data in Figure 1B.

claim: N-terminal tagging did not impair the biological activity of Wnt3a.
source: The Wnt reporter assay revealed that both CM possessed similar activity (Figure 1B), indicating that the N-terminal tagging did not impair the biological activity of Wnt3a that had been successfully secreted into the media.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparable activity shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A 70-kDa protein was reproducibly co-purified with Wnt3a at near stoichiometric fashion.
source: Among them, the 70-kDa protein was reproducibly co-purified with Wnt3a at near stoicheometric fashion, while the amount of 25-kDa protein was generally much lower than Wnt3a and varied among different experiments.
evidence: This is shown in the purification gel in Figure 2.

claim: The 25-kDa band is bovine apolipoprotein A1 (ApoA1).
source: The N-terminal sequence of the 25-kDa band (GDDPQSSWDRV) revealed that it is the bovine apolipoprotein A1 (ApoA1; NP_776667).
evidence: This is determined by N-terminal Edman sequencing.

claim: A part of secreted Wnt3a is released onto ApoA1-containing HDL particles.
source: This is consistent with the report by Neumann et al that a part of secreted Wnt3a is released onto ApoA1-containing HDL particles (Neumann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Neumann et al., 2009.

claim: The 70-kDa band is afamin.
source: In contrast, N-terminal Edman sequencing of the 70-kDa band derived a sequence of LPTQPQDVDD, which was in 100% match with the first 10 residues of a relatively unknown protein called afamin (NP_001179104).
evidence: This is determined by N-terminal Edman sequencing.

claim: Afamin (AFM), also known as α-albumin, is a plasma glycoprotein that belongs to the albumin superfamily proteins.
source: Afamin (AFM), also known as α-albumin, is a plasma glycoprotein that belongs to the albumin superfamily proteins (Lichenstein et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lichenstein et al., 1994.

claim: Little is known about the physiological function of afamin except for its potential role as a carrier of vitamin E.
source: Little is known about the physiological function of this protein except for its potential role as a carrier of vitamin E (Kratzer et al., 2009), and there have been no reports that suggest functional linkage between AFM and Wnts.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kratzer et al., 2009.

claim: There have been no reports that suggest functional linkage between AFM and Wnts prior to this study.
source: Little is known about the physiological function of this protein except for its potential role as a carrier of vitamin E (Kratzer et al., 2009), and there have been no reports that suggest functional linkage between AFM and Wnts.
evidence: This describes the state of knowledge before the current study.

claim: Both tagged and untagged Wnt3a can be co-immunoprecipitated with bovine AFM from the CM.
source: As clearly shown in Figure 3A, both tagged and untagged Wnt3a can be co-immunoprecipitaed with bovine AFM from the CM, indicating that Wnt3a itself but not the tag portion has ability to specifically bind to AFM.
evidence: This is shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3A.

claim: Wnt3a itself but not the tag portion has ability to specifically bind to AFM.
source: As clearly shown in Figure 3A, both tagged and untagged Wnt3a can be co-immunoprecipitaed with bovine AFM from the CM, indicating that Wnt3a itself but not the tag portion has ability to specifically bind to AFM.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation of both tagged and untagged Wnt3a with AFM.

claim: Addition of purified recombinant human AFM into the media restored Wnt3a secretion in a dose dependent manner in serum-free conditions.
source: Remarkably, addition of purified recombinant human AFM into the media restored the Wnt3a secretion in a dose dependent manner, even though the medium contained no other proteins or special additives (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 3B.

claim: Only AFM among albumin superfamily proteins was able to enhance Wnt3a secretion.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, only AFM was able to enhance Wnt3a secretion, suggesting that AFM is the major serum factor responsible for this activity.
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 3C comparing different albumin family proteins.

claim: AFM is the major serum factor responsible for supporting Wnt3a secretion.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, only AFM was able to enhance Wnt3a secretion, suggesting that AFM is the major serum factor responsible for this activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of AFM among albumin family proteins shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Albumin superfamily comprises of four members: serum albumin, AFM, α-fetoprotein (AFP), and vitamin D binding protein (VDBP).
source: Albumin superfamily comprises of four members, including serum albumin, AFM, α-fetoprotein (AFP), and vitamin D binding protein (VDBP), all present in blood at different concentrations (Lichenstein et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lichenstein et al., 1994.

claim: AFM-Wnt interaction is susceptible to detergent treatment.
source: As the critical trick for the successful Wnt purification discovered by Willert et al is the addition of 1% CHAPS at the beginning of the purification steps (Willert, 2008), we speculated that AFM-Wnt interaction may be susceptible to a detergent treatment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: In detergent-free conditions, there is a 100-kDa peak containing both Wnt3a and AFM.
source: In the detergent-free condition (panels labeled as "'– CHAPS"' in Figure 4), however, there is a second peak eluting at 13.6 ml corresponding to the size of ~100 kDa. Coomassie staining (Figure 4C) and anti-Wnt3a immunoblot (Figure 4D) revealed that Wnt3a protein is contained in this 100-kDa peak as well as in the HMW fractions.
evidence: This is shown in the SEC data in Figure 4A and 4C-E.

claim: AFM immunoreactivity was solely present in the 100-kDa peak and not in the HMW fractions.
source: When the same set of samples were probed with anti-AFM antisera, AFM immunoreactivity was solely present in the 100-kDa peak and not in the HMW fractions (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in the immunoblot data in Figure 4E.

claim: The 100-kDa peak represents the stable and monodispersed 1:1 complex formed between Wnt3a and AFM.
source: As the apparent size of this peak (100 kDa) is close to the sum of the molecular masses of Wnt3a (37 kDa) and AFM (70 kDa), we conclude that this peak represents the stable and monodispersed 1:1 complex formed between Wnt3a and AFM.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular weight and composition of the peak shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Wnt3a trapped in HDL particles accounts for at least part of the HMW peak.
source: In contrast to AFM, the 25-kDa ApoA1 antigen was broadly present in the HMW fractions but not in the 13.6-ml peak (Figure 4F), suggesting that the Wnt3a trapped in HDL particles accounts for at least part of the HMW peak.
evidence: This is inferred from the ApoA1 distribution shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The HMW fractions are enriched by Wnt3a oligomers that are covalently crosslinked by disulfide bonds.
source: It also became evident that the HMW fractions are enriched by Wnt3a oligomers that are covalently crosslinked by disulfide bonds, while such oligomers are absent in AFM-containing fractions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in the immunoblot data in Figure 4D.

claim: Wnt3a oligomers are absent in AFM-containing fractions.
source: It also became evident that the HMW fractions are enriched by Wnt3a oligomers that are covalently crosslinked by disulfide bonds, while such oligomers are absent in AFM-containing fractions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in the immunoblot data in Figure 4D.

claim: In the presence of 1% CHAPS, Wnt3a does not co-elute with AFM.
source: In sharp contrast to the results described above, the gel filtration profile obtained in the presence of 1% CHAPS (panels labeled as +CHAPS) shows completely different pattern; the Wnt3a do not co-elute with AFM any more but present in a broad range of fractions centered around ~50 kDa, with a concomitant increase in the covalent oligomer formation (Figures 4B–D).
evidence: This is shown in the SEC data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: The specific interaction between Wnt3a and AFM is lost in the presence of 1% CHAPS.
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that the specific interaction between Wnt3a and AFM is lost in the presence of 1% CHAPS, hence evaded from the discovery of its presence in the previous studies.
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC data comparing +/- CHAPS conditions in Figure 4.

claim: Purified AFM-Wnt3a complex exhibited concentration-dependent induction of reporter in the TCF reporter assay.
source: When the purified AFM-Wnt3a complex dissolved in a CHAPS-free buffer was tested in the Wnt/β-catenin-responsive TCF reporter assay using HEK293 cells stably expressing luciferase gene under the control of TCF/LEF, concentration-dependent induction of reporter was observed (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: This is shown in the reporter assay data in Figure 5A.

claim: Positive signal was detected at concentration as low as 0.56 nM (20 ng/ml) for AFM-Wnt3a complex.
source: The positive signal was detected at concentration as low as 0.56 nM (20 ng/ml), and reached the saturation at around 15 nM (500 ng/ml).
evidence: This is shown in the reporter assay data in Figure 5A.

claim: Commercially available carrier-free Wnt3a protein exhibited much lower activity than AFM-Wnt3a complex in the TCF reporter assay.
source: In contrast, commercially available carrier-free Wnt3a protein (R&D Systems, purified according to the method by Willert et al. (Willert, 2008)) exhibited much lower activity in the same assay condition (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: This is shown in the reporter assay data in Figure 5A comparing the two preparations.

claim: The EC50 value for the AFM-Wnt3a complex is estimated to be 5~10-fold lower than that for the purified Wnt3a.
source: Assuming that the maximum reporter induction achievable by two different Wnt3a preparations is identical, the EC50 value for the AFM-Wnt3a complex is estimated to be 5~10-fold lower than that for the purified Wnt3a.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-response curves in Figure 5A.

claim: AFM-Wnt3a complex exhibited similar activity before and after storage at 4°C for 1 month in PBS.
source: Furthermore, AFM-Wnt3a complex exhibited similar activity before and after the storage at 4°C for 1 month in PBS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating the stable nature of this preparation in the absence of any detergents.
evidence: This is shown in the stability data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: AFM-Wnt3a complex preparation is stable in the absence of any detergents.
source: Furthermore, AFM-Wnt3a complex exhibited similar activity before and after the storage at 4°C for 1 month in PBS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating the stable nature of this preparation in the absence of any detergents.
evidence: This is inferred from the stability data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Active Wnt3a signal is required for the stem cells present at the bottom of the intestinal crypt to self-renew.
source: Active Wnt3a signal is required for the stem cells present at the bottom of the intestinal crypt to self-renew (Sato and Clevers, 2013), and it is established that human colonic organoids require a set of growth factors (including Wnt3a, EGF, noggin, and R-spondin-1) for sustained expansion (Sato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sato and Clevers, 2013 and Sato et al., 2011.

claim: Human colonic organoids require a set of growth factors (including Wnt3a, EGF, noggin, and R-spondin-1) for sustained expansion.
source: Active Wnt3a signal is required for the stem cells present at the bottom of the intestinal crypt to self-renew (Sato and Clevers, 2013), and it is established that human colonic organoids require a set of growth factors (including Wnt3a, EGF, noggin, and R-spondin-1) for sustained expansion (Sato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sato et al., 2011.

claim: Purified Wnt3a from a commercial source failed to support organoid expansion when added at 300 ng/ml.
source: However, purified Wnt3a obtained from a commercial source failed to show this activity when added at 300 ng/ml to the culture (Figure 5B, Wnt3a(R&D)).
evidence: This is shown in the organoid culture data in Figure 5B.

claim: CHAPS-purified Wnt3a loses its activity upon prolonged incubation at 37°C.
source: This result is consistent with the finding by Dhamdhere et al that CHAPS-purified Wnt3a lose its activity upon prolonged incubation at 37°C (Dhamdhere et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dhamdhere et al., 2014.

claim: AFM-Wnt3a complex was able to support organoid expansion at 300 ng/ml.
source: In contrast, AFM-Wnt3a complex was able to support organoid expansion at the same concentration (Figure 5B, Wnt3a:AFM, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the organoid culture data in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Organoids were able to expand for more than 18 passages over a period of 4 months when supplemented with AFM-Wnt3a complex.
source: When supplemented with the same concentration of AFM-Wnt3a complex in the medium for each passage, organoids were able to expand for more than 18 passages over a period of 4 months (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Tg-Wnt5a co-purified with serum afamin by anti-tag immunoaffinity chromatography.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, Tg-Wnt5a co-purified with serum afamin by the anti-tag immunoaffinity chromatography, just like Wnt3a (compare with Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in the purification gel in Figure 6A.

claim: The SEC profile of immunopurified Wnt5a preparation was essentially the same as that of Wnt3a, showing the presence of monodispersed AFM-Wnt5a complex peak.
source: Furthermore, the SEC profile of the immunopurified Wnt5a preparation was essentially the same as that of Wnt3a, showing the presence of monodispersed AFM-Wnt5a complex peak eluting at around 150 kDa, in addition to the HMW aggregate fractions (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the SEC data in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The AFM-Wnt5a complex induced phosphorylation of Dvl2 in NIH3T3 cells at concentrations above 10 ng/ml.
source: Finally, the AFM-Wnt5a complex thus purified was biologically active, because it induced phosphorylation of Dvl2 in NIH3T3 cells at concentrations above 10 ng/ml (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in the Dvl2 phosphorylation assay in Figure 6C.

claim: The activity of AFM-Wnt5a complex was indistinguishable with that of AFM-free Wnt5a protein freshly purified from the CM.
source: Importantly, the activity of AFM-Wnt5a complex was indistinguishable with that of AFM-free Wnt5a protein freshly purified from the CM using the conventional method (Kurayoshi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is shown in the Dvl2 phosphorylation assay in Figure 6C comparing the two preparations.

claim: Transient transfection of PA-Wnt3a alone into Expi293F cells did not result in the secretion of Wnt3a.
source: Transient transfection of PA-Wnt3a alone into the suspension culture of Expi293F cells did not result in the secretion of Wnt3a (Figure 7A. lane 1), which was expected because the culture medium for this cell line did not contain serum.
evidence: This is shown in the gel in Figure 7A.

claim: Co-transfection of PA-Wnt3a with human AFM resulted in visible Wnt3a secretion.
source: In contrast, when the cells were co-transfected with PA-Wnt3a and human AFM, ~37-kDa Wnt3a band became visible in the NZ-1 immunoprecipitates along with the associated AFM (Figure 7A, lane 2), confirming the ability of AFM to enhance Wnt production/secretion by co-expression.
evidence: This is shown in the gel in Figure 7A.

claim: Out of 19 PA-tagged human Wnts, 12 members could be secreted at detectable level from HEK293T cells when transfected alone in the presence of serum.
source: Out of the 19 PA-tagged human Wnts, 12 members (Wnt1, Wnt2b, Wnt3, Wnt3a, Wnt5a, Wnt7a, Wnt7b, Wnt8a, Wnt9a, Wnt9b, Wnt10a, and Wnt10b) could be secreted at detectable level from HEK293T cells when transfected alone in the presence of serum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the immunoblot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: 12 human Wnt proteins exhibited no or very little secretion into serum-free culture media when singly transfected into Expi293F cells.
source: As in the case of mouse Wnt3a, 12 human Wnt proteins exhibited no or very little secretion into the serum-free culture media when singly transfected into the Expi293F cells (Figure 7B, lanes marked with –).
evidence: This is shown in the immunoblot data in Figure 7B.

claim: Expression of 12 human Wnt proteins was enhanced upon co-transfection with human AFM.
source: However, their expression was enhanced upon the co-transfection with human AFM (Figure 7B, lanes marked with +).
evidence: This is shown in the immunoblot data in Figure 7B.

claim: All tested Wnts directly associated with AFM as evidenced by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Although the extent of the enhancement varied among different Wnts, all Wnts directly associated with AFM as evidenced by the co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 7C), suggesting that AFM can serve as a secretion vehicle for most if not all Wnt proteins to aid their simple purification.
evidence: This is shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7C.

claim: AFM can serve as a secretion vehicle for most if not all Wnt proteins to aid their simple purification.
source: Although the extent of the enhancement varied among different Wnts, all Wnts directly associated with AFM as evidenced by the co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 7C), suggesting that AFM can serve as a secretion vehicle for most if not all Wnt proteins to aid their simple purification.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7C.

claim: Only Wnt3 and Wnt3a showed significant activity in the TCF reporter assay among the tested Wnts.
source: As shown in Figure 7D, only Wnt3 and Wnt3a showed significant activity in this assay system.
evidence: This is shown in the reporter assay data in Figure 7D.

claim: ~170 µg mouse Wnt3a and ~120 µg human Wnt3 were obtained from a 300 ml culture media.
source: Typically, we obtained ~170 µg mouse Wnt3a and ~120 µg human Wnt3 from a 300 ml culture media.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the large-scale purification experiments.

claim: The AFM-Wnt3a/3 complex produced from cells upon co-expression primarily behaved as a monodispersed molecular species.
source: As in the case of AFM-Wnt complex formed in the serum-containing culture media (i.e., Figures 2 and 6), the AFM-Wnt3a/3 complex produced from cells upon co-expression primarily behaved as a monodispersed molecular species (Figure 8B,C, fraction II).
evidence: This is shown in the SEC data in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: Both Wnt3a and Wnt3 are not present in the HMW peak when produced by co-expression in serum-free media.
source: Furthermore, both Wnts are not present in the HMW peak (fraction I), suggesting that the absence of serum components in the culture media is advantageous to obtain cleaner Wnt samples devoid of contaminating proteins such as HDL.
evidence: This is shown in the SEC data in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: The absence of serum components in the culture media is advantageous to obtain cleaner Wnt samples devoid of contaminating proteins such as HDL.
source: Furthermore, both Wnts are not present in the HMW peak (fraction I), suggesting that the absence of serum components in the culture media is advantageous to obtain cleaner Wnt samples devoid of contaminating proteins such as HDL.
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC data in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: AFM-Wnt3a and AFM-Wnt3 complexes produced by co-expression were active in the Wnt/β-catenin signaling reporter assay.
source: Finally, we confirmed that AFM-Wnt3a as well as AFM-Wnt3 complexes thus produced were active in the Wnt/β-catenin signaling reporter assay, exhibiting similar concentration dependency with that of AFM-Wnt3a complex purified from serum-containing CM (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This is shown in the reporter assay data in Figure 8D and 8E.

claim: The lipid modification of Wnt was identified as an acylation of conserved Ser residue with palmitoleic acid.
source: The most enigmatic character of Wnt proteins is their hydrophobic nature due to the covalent lipid modification discovered by Willert et al (Willert et al., 2003), which was later identified by Takada and colleagues as an acylation of conserved Ser residue with palmitoleic acid (Takada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Willert et al., 2003 and Takada et al., 2006.

claim: Garcia and colleagues determined the crystal structure of Xenopus Wnt8.
source: The next breakthrough in the Wnt preparation was brought by Garcia and colleagues, who determined the crystal structure of Xenopus Wnt8 (Janda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Janda et al., 2012.

claim: Wnt8 protein was expressed as a stable and tight complex with a fragment of its receptor Frizzled8 (Fz8).
source: They expressed Wnt8 protein as a stable and tight complex with a fragment of its receptor Frizzled8 (Fz8), which sequestered the problematic acyl chain and increased the solubility of the complex.
evidence: This is supported by the citation context referring to the work by Garcia and colleagues.

claim: Notum is an extracellular deacylase that removes the palmitoleic acid attached to the conserved Ser residue in Wnt3a.
source: In fact, Kakugawa et al have recently reported an extracellular deacylase called Notum, which removes the palmitoleic acid attached to the conserved Ser residue in Wnt3a (Kakugawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kakugawa et al., 2015.

claim: Deacylated Wnt lacks biological activity.
source: However, the resultant deacylated Wnt, although it may be water-soluble, lacks biological activity and its utility in the structure-function analysis is limited.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of Notum-treated Wnt.

claim: Liposome-packaged Wnt3a has long life at 37°C and may potentially be suitable for in vivo delivery.
source: Although the liposome-packaged Wnt3a have long life at 37°C and may potentially be suitable for the in vivo delivery (Dhamdhere et al., 2014), one still needs to produce large quantity of CHAPS-solubilized Wnt proteins, which remains technically demanding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dhamdhere et al., 2014.

claim: AFM uses its unique lipid-binding pocket to bind and sequester the palmitoleic moiety of Wnt proteins.
source: The facts that 1) only AFM but not other three albumin family proteins can capture Wnts and 2) the interaction between AFM and Wnt is completely disrupted by 1% CHAPS seem to indicate that AFM uses its unique lipid-binding pocket to bind and sequester the palmitoleic moiety of Wnt proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity and detergent sensitivity of the interaction.

claim: The affinity of AFM to the fatty acid is strong enough to make stable complex with lipid-modified Wnt but weaker than that of Fz CRD.
source: We speculate that the affinity of AFM to the fatty acid is strong enough to make stable complex with lipid-modified Wnt but weaker than that of Fz CRD, enabling it to 'deliver' the ligand to the receptor at the cell surface.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain how AFM-Wnt complex can be biologically active.

claim: AFM is primarily synthesized in the liver.
source: AFM, as other albumin family proteins, is primarily synthesized in the liver and present not only in blood but also in other adult body fluids including cerebrospinal, ovarian follicular, and seminal fluids (Dieplinger and Dieplinger, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dieplinger and Dieplinger, 2015.

claim: AFM is present not only in blood but also in other adult body fluids including cerebrospinal, ovarian follicular, and seminal fluids.
